test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 23 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: Which of the following is true for mixtures but NOT for compounds?

options.text: Components are present in fixed ratio.
Components can be separated by physical methods.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Components can be separated by physical methods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Physical Separation**: The primary distinction between a mixture and a compound is the method of separation. Components of a **mixture** can be separated using **physical methods** such as **filtration**, **evaporation**, **distillation**, **crystallization**, or **magnetization** because the substances are only physically blended. ***Hence, the statement "Components can be separated by physical methods" is true for mixtures.***
 
• **Fixed Ratio**: In a **compound**, elements are always present in a **fixed ratio by mass** (according to the **Law of Definite Proportions**). In contrast, the components of a **mixture** can be combined in **any proportion**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect for mixtures.***
 
• **Formation of New Substances**: A **compound** is a new substance formed through a **chemical reaction** where the constituent elements lose their identity. In a **mixture**, no **chemical bond** is formed, and thus no new chemical substance is created. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect for mixtures.***
 
• **Retention of Properties**: In a **mixture**, each constituent substance **retains its individual chemical and physical properties** (e.g., sugar in water still tastes sweet). In a **compound**, the properties of the product are entirely **different** from its constituent elements (e.g., **Water (H2O)** is a liquid, while **Hydrogen** and **Oxygen** are gases). ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect for mixtures.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mixtures**: 
 
 
• A **mixture** contains two or more substances that are not chemically combined. 
 
• They are classified into two types: **Homogeneous mixtures** (uniform composition, e.g., **air**, **alloys** like **brass**) and **Heterogeneous mixtures** (non-uniform composition, e.g., **sand and salt**, **oil and water**).
 
• There is **no energy change** (absorption or evolution of heat/light) typically associated with the formation of a mixture.
 
 
 
• **Compounds**:
 
 
• A **compound** is a substance formed when two or more chemical elements are **chemically bonded** together.
 
• The types of bonds can be **covalent** or **ionic**.
 
• Compounds have a **fixed melting point** and **boiling point**, whereas mixtures show a range of temperatures.
 
• Separation of compounds requires **chemical** or **electrochemical reactions** like **electrolysis**.
 
 
 
• **Examples**:
 
 
• **Common Salt (NaCl)** is a **compound**; it cannot be separated into **Sodium** and **Chlorine** by simple filtration.
 
• **Gunpowder** is a **mixture** of **nitre (potassium nitrate)**, **sulphur**, and **charcoal**, which can be separated using solvents or physical means.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Energy Changes**: The formation of a **compound** involves a significant **change in energy**, usually in the form of **heat**, **light**, or **sound**. Mixtures are formed with little to no detectable energy change.
 
• **Homogeneity**: While all **compounds** are **homogeneous** in nature, **mixtures** can be either **homogeneous** or **heterogeneous**.
 
• **Identity**: The constituents of a **compound** lose their **chemical identity**, whereas the constituents of a **mixture** do not. For example, **Iron (Fe)** and **Sulphur (S)** mixed together can be separated by a magnet, but when heated to form **Iron Sulphide (FeS)**, the magnet no longer attracts the iron.
